title: Your own loneliness
hook: Jesus was alone in Gethsemane too
tomorrow: Jesus knew he'd raise Lazarus. so why did he cry?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a dinner where Jesus redrew the guest list: call the poor, and keep a chair for someone who can't repay you. The line was open table. Today, the lonely one might be you.

A full room can be the loneliest place there is: everyone talking, nobody asking how you are. On the night before he dies, Jesus walks out to a garden called Gethsemane, and he takes three friends further in with him, Peter, James and John. He tells them, in the Douay-Rheims Bible, "My soul is sorrowful even unto death: stay you here, and watch with me." Then he goes on a little way, falls on his face, and prays. When he comes back, they're asleep.
screen: `LONELY IN A FULL ROOM.` → `WATCH WITH ME.` → `THEY'RE ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: So why bring them? Matthew's answer is right there: watch with me. Jesus doesn't ask them to fix anything or find the right words. He asks for company in the dark: not a speech, not a plan, just someone awake nearby. And they sleep. This is the same evening Peter promised he'd die with Jesus before he'd ever deny him. He wakes Peter: "What? Could you not watch one hour with me?" Three times he goes off to pray, and three times he comes back to find them sleeping. Matthew doesn't smooth it over. The loneliness is real, even for him, even with friends a few steps away. One to tell a friend: Catholics have answered that question with an hour. Some keep a holy hour of prayer, a practice linked to those words, and on Holy Thursday night the Church keeps watch after the evening Mass, staying with him in the garden. So the lonely night isn't hidden at the edge of the story. It sits near the center, and he has been there first, face to the ground.
screen: `COMPANY, NOT ANSWERS.` · `COULD YOU NOT WATCH ONE HOUR?` · `THREE TIMES, ASLEEP.` · `A HOLY HOUR IN REPLY.` · then, large: `NOT ALONE IN IT.`

segments.voice: Take the posture of the garden. Kneel if you can, or sit and let your head bow toward your knees, hands open, and feel the floor take your weight. Let whatever is lonely in you be there, without explaining it or rushing it off. If you pray, you can bring it as it is, to the one who asked his friends to stay; if not, simply stay with it, the way he asked them to.
Your own loneliness. The ache of feeling unaccompanied, which the Gospel places in Gethsemane, with Jesus himself. Today's word.
Your line: not alone in it. Jesus knew that garden, and that sleeping circle of friends, before you did. Go gently.

chat.meaning: In Gethsemane, Jesus's friends were a little way off, asleep. Loneliness can come in a full room, and he has been there too.

notes: Matthew 26:38 and 26:40 quoted from Douay-Rheims; confirm exact wording and punctuation ('What? Could you not watch one hour with me?').
'Three friends': Matthew 26:37 names Peter and the two sons of Zebedee; James and John are named in Mark 14:33. Confirm the naming is acceptable here.
'Three times he goes off to pray... finds them sleeping': Matthew 26:40, 43, 44–45. Confirm.

Holy hour 'a practice linked to those words' (devotion associated with Matthew 26:40 and St. Margaret Mary Alacoque, not named). Holy Thursday watch after the Mass of the Lord's Supper (altar of repose). Confirm wording.
